title: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed (balanced) parentheses.
shortTitle: Generate Parentheses: track open and close counts
keyPoints: Backtrack with two counters: open count and close count, building the string character by character.
Place an open parenthesis while open < n; place a close only while close < open.
The close < open invariant ensures no prefix ever has more closes than opens, so every string is valid.
The number of valid strings is the nth Catalan number, far fewer than the 2^(2n) brute-force candidates.
Use StringBuilder with append-recurse-delete for efficient backtracking without string allocation.
This generate-only-valid-states approach avoids wasted work and is a general backtracking optimization.

s1_definition.oneliner: Open while open < n, close while close < open, record at length 2n; never generate an invalid string.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Generate Parentheses** – produce every well-formed string of n open and n close parentheses using constrained backtracking.
- **Two rules** – append `(` while `open < n`; append `)` only while `close < open`.
- **Invariant** – `close < open` guarantees every prefix stays valid, so no validity check is needed at the end.
- **Count** – the number of results is the nth Catalan number.
- **Backtracking** – append one character, recurse, then delete the last character to undo.
- **Efficiency** – only valid strings are ever built, avoiding the exponential waste of generate-then-filter.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, an approval-rule builder lets designers compose nested approval brackets, where an opener starts a sub-approval and a closer finishes it. For n levels, the tool enumerates every valid nesting pattern. A designer writes the pattern left to right: she can start a new sub-approval as long as she has starts remaining, and she can finish one only if there is an unfinished one open. Every pattern she writes is valid by construction.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Backtracking Tree for n=2
  ──────────────────────────

                    ""
                   / 
                  (
                /   \
              ((     ()
              |      |
             (()    ()(
              |      |
             (())   ()()

  Results: "(())", "()()"
  Only valid branches explored
```

```text
  Decision at each node
  ──────────────────────
  Can I place '(' ?  →  open < n
  Can I place ')' ?  →  close < open
  Am I done?         →  length == 2n

  Both conditions can be true → two branches
  Only one true → one branch
  Neither true → impossible (never happens)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Generate Parentheses is a backtracking problem where the elegance comes from never building an invalid string. I track two counters, how many opens and how many closes I have placed, and I build the string one character at a time. I may append an open parenthesis while the open count is below n, and I may append a close only when the close count is strictly less than the open count. When the string reaches length 2n, it is guaranteed balanced.

The `close < open` invariant is the key. It ensures that at every point in the string, the number of closes never exceeds the number of opens, which means every prefix stays valid. Because invalid prefixes are never built, every leaf of the recursion is a valid string, and the total count is the nth Catalan number, which is dramatically fewer than the 2^(2n) candidates a brute-force approach would generate.

I use `StringBuilder` with append-recurse-deleteCharAt for efficient backtracking. String concatenation would allocate a new object on every recursive call, which is much slower. The delete step after recursion restores the builder for the next branch, and forgetting it is a classic bug that corrupts subsequent results.

In my project at the National Bank of India, this constrained backtracking generated all valid nesting templates for an approval-rule builder, so the governance team could review every possible workflow shape. Enforcing the two placement rules during construction guaranteed every template was valid by construction.

Remember one sentence: place an open while opens remain, place a close only while closes trail opens, and the result is every valid combination with no wasted generation.
